data: In broad continuity with the course Introduction to Comparative Politics, this course involves a deeper engagement with the key themes and methodological approaches that constitute the dynamic field of Comparative Politics. This course offers an advanced exploration of conceptual variables such as state formation and state capacity, social movements, and civil society as well as ideologically conditioned political processes such as democratisation, and development across supra-national, national, and local levels. The thematic composition of this course is informed by gender and intersectional lenses. Beginning with the evolution of the field beyond its Euro-American moorings, the course will delve into the diverse methods that characterise comparative research. This is followed by a historically contextualised study of dominant political ideologies. Other key themes covered in the course include political parties, representative democracy, and contemporary phenomena such as populism.
